title: Physically Based Rendering: From Theory to Implementation, 4th ed. — §9.3 Specular Reflection and Transmission; §11.1 Volume Scattering Processes
authors: Matt Pharr, Wenzel Jakob, Greg Humphreys
key_findings: Table 9.1 IOR: air 1.00029, ice 1.31, water 1.333, fused quartz 1.46, glass 1.5-1.6, sapphire 1.77, diamond 2.42
Critical angle for air-glass TIR roughly 42 degrees
Conductors use complex IOR; light absorbed within ~0.1 micrometre
Media: sigma_t = sigma_a + sigma_s; transmittance falls exponentially; single-scattering albedo = sigma_s/sigma_t; mean free path = 1/sigma_t
practical_applications: Lens Fresnel/TIR table in LIGHTING_PHYSICS
Volumetric light and fog vocabulary
limitations: Extends registry record PBRT4 (which was bibliographic only): two sections read in full this session; other chapters not read

title: Physically-Based Shading at Disney (SIGGRAPH 2012 course notes v3)
key_findings: Principles: intuitive not physical parameters, as few as possible, 0-1 over plausible range
Parameters: baseColor, subsurface, metallic, specular, specularTint, roughness, anisotropic, sheen, sheenTint, clearcoat, clearcoatGloss
specular 0-1 maps to incident specular 0-0.08 = IOR 1.0-1.8; 0.5 = IOR 1.5 default
Clearcoat fixed IOR 1.5 (polyurethane)
alpha = roughness^2 for perceptual linearity
Diffuse is tinted by subsurface absorption; specular not tinted unless metallic
MERL observations: some woods show specular modulation; fabrics odd grazing response
practical_applications: PBR parameter table; rule: non-metal highlights are white
limitations: Extends registry record Burley2012 (publisher page only); full notes read this session via PDF text extraction; production model, art-directable rather than strictly physical

title: Real Shading in Unreal Engine 4 (SIGGRAPH 2013 course notes)
key_findings: Base material: BaseColor, Metallic, Roughness, Cavity; Specular dropped, non-metal F0 constant 0.04
Variable IOR 'fairly unimportant for nonmetals'
Physically accurate inverse-square falloff windowed: saturate(1-(d/r)^4)^2/(d^2+1)
Sphere and tube area lights via representative point with energy conservation so materials look the same regardless of light size
practical_applications: Falloff explanation; why eyewear lenses are an exception to constant F0
limitations: Real-time production notes (industry); not peer reviewed

title: Background: Physics and Math of Shading (SIGGRAPH 2013 course notes)
key_findings: Absorption, scattering and their combination set appearance; white = high scattering + low absorption
Ordinary diffuse is subsurface scattering at a scale smaller than a pixel
Schlick Fresnel F0 + (1-F0)(1-cos)^5; zones 0-45 / 45-75 / 75-90 degrees; red zone visible only at extreme edges

F0 table (from RTR3): water 0.02, plastic/glass low 0.03, plastic high 0.05, glass high/ruby 0.08, diamond 0.17, iron 0.56-0.58, copper 0.95/0.64/0.54, gold 1.00/0.71/0.29, aluminium 0.91-0.92, silver 0.95/0.93/0.88
Non-metals outside labs mostly 2-5% F0
practical_applications: F0 values in material library; prompt rule against 'highly reflective acetate'
limitations: Course notes hosted on a university teaching mirror

title: Real-Time Rendering, 4th ed.
authors: Tomas Akenine-Möller, Eric Haines, Naty Hoffman, Angelo Pesce, Michał Iwanicki, Sébastien Hillaire
key_findings: Chapters include 7 Shadows, 8 Light and Color, 9 Physically Based Shading, 10 Local Illumination, 11 Global Illumination, 14 Volumetric and Translucency Rendering, 15 Non-Photorealistic Rendering
practical_applications: Pointer for deeper reading on shadows, GI, volumetrics
limitations: Only the book's website/table of contents read; content not read

title: Optics, 5th ed.
key_findings: Standard optics textbook: propagation of light, geometrical optics, polarization, interference, diffraction (chapter list)
practical_applications: Reference for Fresnel/polarization/thin-film interference foundations
limitations: Bibliographic only (publisher listing); dates differ 2016/2017 between listings; no content cited from it

title: Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces
authors: Bruce Walter, Stephen R. Marschner, Hongsong Li, Kenneth E. Torrance
key_findings: Extends microfacet theory to rough transmission (e.g. etched/ground glass)
Introduces GGX distribution, closer match than Beckmann for some surfaces
GGX later identified with Trowbridge-Reitz
practical_applications: Frosted glass / satin acetate vocabulary; roughness on transmissive materials
limitations: Abstract and secondary descriptions only

title: Measuring and Modeling Anisotropic Reflection
key_findings: Introduces a reflectance measurement device and a mathematical model of anisotropic reflectance, fitted to measured surfaces
practical_applications: Brushed metal/hair anisotropy vocabulary
limitations: Only the abstract was readable; highlight direction vs groove direction NOT confirmed from this source

title: Production Friendly Microfacet Sheen BRDF
key_findings: Cheap, artist-friendly sheen lobe for cloth; layered via albedo scaling
Its distribution ('Charlie') adopted by glTF KHR_materials_sheen
practical_applications: Velvet/fabric sheen parameter in material library
limitations: Search summary only

title: Light Scattering from Human Hair Fibers
authors: Stephen R. Marschner, Henrik Wann Jensen, Mike Cammarano, Steve Worley, Pat Hanrahan
key_findings: Fibre modelled as transparent elliptical cylinder with absorbing interior and tilted scales
Lobes R (surface), TT (transmission), TRT (internal reflection, secondary highlight)
Secondary highlight not present in black hair
practical_applications: Hair highlight rules for characters
limitations: Abstract + secondary excerpts; full paper not read

title: GPU Gems 3, Chapter 14: Advanced Techniques for Realistic Real-Time Skin Rendering
key_findings: Skin: oily layer + epidermis (narrow scatter) + dermis (wide scatter)
Specular F0 = 0.028 from assumed IOR 1.4; skin specular should be white
Red scatters much farther than green/blue (red profile ~16 mm wide in model)
Without SSS skin looks hard and dry; errors cause red glow around shadows, waxy ears
practical_applications: Skin rendering rules and AI artefact checks
limitations: Real-time technique chapter; final ~10% of page not read; author names from general knowledge of the book, page header not quoted

title: KHR_materials_ior (glTF 2.0 extension specification)
key_findings: Default ior 1.5; dielectric_f0 = ((ior-1)/(ior+1))^2 = 0.04 at 1.5
Example IORs: air 1.0, water 1.33, eyes 1.38, window glass 1.52, sapphire 1.76, diamond 2.42
practical_applications: F0 formula used to compute lens reflectance table
limitations: Year is approximate (extension ratification); page date not checked

title: KHR_materials_volume (glTF 2.0 extension specification)
key_findings: thicknessFactor 0 = thin-walled; non-zero = volumetric (closed mesh)
attenuationColor/attenuationDistance: sigma_t = -ln(c)/d; T(x) = c^(x/d) (Beer-Lambert, scattering assumed zero)
Refraction requires KHR_materials_transmission; IOR default 1.5
practical_applications: Absorption rule: thicker coloured lens/acetate = darker; transmission vs opacity distinction
limitations: Year approximate; license as stated in repo not re-checked

title: OpenPBR Surface specification
key_findings: Defaults: base_color 0.8, specular_roughness 0.3, specular_ior 1.5 (range 1-3), transmission_dispersion_abbe_number 20 (range 9-91)
subsurface_radius_scale default (1.0, 0.5, 0.25)
Thin-film thickness (micrometres) and IOR control intensity, spacing and hue of colour fringes
Higher Abbe number = less dispersion
practical_applications: Thin-film = AR/mirror coatings; dispersion for PC lenses; parameter vocabulary
limitations: Only first ~100k of 177k characters read; coat/fuzz/geometry defaults not read; year approximate

title: Physically Based — the PBR values database
key_findings: Linear colours + IOR: water 1.333; marble, concrete, office paper, porcelain 1.5; diamond 2.417; milk 1.348; ice 1.31
practical_applications: Base colour starting points in material library
limitations: Several entries (glass, titanium, skin, plastic) shown without values in fetched text; community-curated

title: Dispersion properties of optical polymers (polycarbonate data on refractiveindex.info)
authors: N. Sultanova, S. Kasarova, I. Nikolov
key_findings: Polycarbonate n ~1.585 at 587.6 nm from Sellmeier fit (Polyanskiy)
practical_applications: Polycarbonate lens IOR
limitations: Read via refractiveindex.info data page, not the paper; Abbe not given there

title: N-BK7 optical glass data (SCHOTT catalogue via refractiveindex.info)
authors: SCHOTT AG; compiled by M. Polyanskiy
practical_applications: Reference crown glass value; distinguishes optical crown from ophthalmic crown 1.523
limitations: Not an ophthalmic lens glass datasheet

title: MR series lineup (lens monomers)
key_findings: Values are representative, not guaranteed specifications
practical_applications: High-index lens IOR and Abbe values
limitations: Manufacturer marketing page; ve (e-line) Abbe, not vd

title: CR-39 (Wikipedia) and PPG CR-39 monomer page — search summary
key_findings: Name from Columbia Resin #39 (1940 project); PPG trademark; first CR-39 spectacle lenses credited to Armorlite, 1947
practical_applications: CR-39 lens IOR
limitations: Search summary only; history dates rest on Wikipedia

title: Spectacle lens material comparisons (All About Vision; Ophthalmology Times) — search summary
key_findings: CR-39 ~1.498 / Abbe 58; polycarbonate 1.586 / ~30; Trivex 1.53 (some 1.54) / 43-45; high-index 1.60-1.74; crown glass ~1.523 / 58-59
Higher index reflects more; some high-index reflect up to 50% more than CR-39
practical_applications: Lens table cross-check
limitations: Consumer/trade sources; discrepancies between them; search summary only

title: Anti-reflection coating residual colour (US patents 8425035 'colour-neutral AR coating', 7311938) and Zeiss coating pages — search summary
key_findings: Finite layers cannot cancel reflection over the whole spectrum -> coloured residual reflection
Usual spectacle AR has green residual reflection (peak near eye sensitivity ~555 nm)
Multilayer stacks reduce total reflectance to <1-2%; per-surface ~0.75-1.5% at 500 nm cited
practical_applications: AR residual colour reveal setup; rule to match residual colour to the real lens
limitations: Search summary; the uncoated '8%' figure not found in these sources (computed from Fresnel instead)

title: Brewster's angle
key_findings: theta_B = arctan(n2/n1); ~56 degrees for air-glass
Polarizing filters remove reflections from water/glass; rotating the polarizer removes polarized reflected light
practical_applications: CPL use on lenses at oblique angles
limitations: Encyclopedia; physics is textbook-standard

title: Cross Polarization: What It Is and Why It Matters; Derek Flood cross-polarization for textures — search summary
key_findings: Polarizer on light + polarizer on lens rotated perpendicular cancels specular reflection (still polarized after bouncing)
Process is not perfect
practical_applications: eyewear_cross_polarized_flat setup
limitations: Search summary; page itself not fetched

title: The perception of cast shadows
authors: Pascal Mamassian, David C. Knill, Daniel Kersten
key_findings: Cast shadows inform object shape, receiving-surface shape and spatial layout; strongest for spatial arrangement, especially when shadows move
Visual system likely assumes a stationary light source
practical_applications: Moving shadow = levitation cue in 2.5D clips; never move the light with the object
limitations: Abstract only

title: Light and Form, Part 1 (Gurney Journey blog)
key_findings: Form principle: analyse nature as geometric solids rendered by tonal contrast
Terms: center light, light/dark halftones, terminator (light tangent to form), highlight (reflection of source, not always at center light), cast shadow
Soft source -> gradual terminator; sun -> strong division
Comments: core usually just past terminator, not always present; darkest spot often the contact crack; 'model the lights or the shadows, not both'
practical_applications: Light-on-form sequence; charcoal three-value plan
limitations: Practitioner blog; some rules come from reader comments endorsed by the author. Gurney2010 book is a separate registry record

title: Elements of Light and Shadow (course notes)
key_findings: Highlight: reflection of the source on shiny surfaces, absent on matte
Center light, halftones, terminator, core shadow (darkest part of form shadow near terminator), reflected light, cast shadow, occlusion shadow (darkest, in crevices)
practical_applications: Shadow family table
limitations: Practitioner teaching; no date

title: Water Reflections, Part 1 (Gurney Journey blog)
key_findings: Light tones reflect a little darker because some light enters the water
Water is near-perfect mirror only at a shallow viewing angle; looking steeply down little sky is reflected
practical_applications: Water reflection rules mapped to Fresnel
limitations: Practitioner; vertical alignment and ripples not covered in this post

title: Light — Science & Magic: An Introduction to Photographic Lighting (6th ed. adds Robin Reid)
authors: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver, Paul Fuqua
key_findings: 'Family of angles' = light positions that produce direct reflection; a larger source fills more of it
Glass chapter: bright-field and dark-field lighting; using both simultaneously causes most glass-photography failures
practical_applications: Eyewear lens/metal reflection planning; dark-field/bright-field rules
limitations: Only previews and search summaries; edition years differ

title: Inverse-square law and the five-times rule for extended sources (CIE 2025 paper by Dotreppe et al.; PetaPixel 2021; photometry teaching notes) — search summary
key_findings: Inverse-square valid only beyond the limiting photometric distance, which depends on source size, intensity distribution, luminance distribution and acceptable error
Minimum test distance 5x largest source dimension for near-Lambertian sources; at 10x radius error ~1%
Ignoring the rule gave deviations up to 32% for task lighting
practical_applications: Large-softbox exception to inverse square
limitations: Search summary across several sources; CIE paper not read

title: A Practical Analytic Model for Daylight
authors: A. J. Preetham, Peter Shirley, Brian Smits
key_findings: Rayleigh extinction ~ lambda^-4, verified experimentally; blue (400 nm) scattered ~10x red (700 nm); low sun yellow/orange from longer path
Haze = more scattering than molecules, less than fog; Mie particles scatter more uniformly -> whitening
Turbidity = (haze+molecular optical thickness)/molecular; linked to meteorological range (contrast threshold 0.02)
Cites psychology: aerial perspective a fundamental depth cue and the only absolute cue for distant unfamiliar objects; Leonardo's observations: horizon whitening, density near ground, hue shift
practical_applications: Aerial perspective, haze and turbidity control in scenes
limitations: Model has known weaknesses addressed by Hosek-Wilkie 2012

title: Precomputed Atmospheric Scattering
key_findings: Real-time Rayleigh+Mie multiple scattering from ground to space
Sky colour in daylight and twilight, aerial perspective for all view/sun directions, earth and mountain shadows as light shafts
practical_applications: Physics behind light shafts and twilight sky
limitations: Abstract only

title: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, ed. J. P. Richter, §295 (aerial perspective)
authors: Leonardo da Vinci; ed. Jean Paul Richter
key_findings: Distant things appear blue 'in consequence of the great quantity of atmosphere between your eye and them'
'if one is to be five times as distant, make it five times bluer'
practical_applications: Painter's rule mapped to exponential extinction
limitations: Translation-dependent wording; one passage read

title: Aerial perspective (Encyclopaedia Britannica) — search summary
key_findings: Leonardo first used the term in the Treatise on Painting
Short wavelengths scattered most, so distant dark objects tend toward blue
Leonardo thought air not blue itself but water vapour lit by sun in front of dark mountains
practical_applications: Aerial perspective history
limitations: Page returned 403; search summary only

title: Crepuscular rays (Atmospheric Optics)
key_findings: Crepuscular rays: sunbeams through cloud gaps separated by shadowed bands; divergence is a perspective illusion
Anticrepuscular rays appear opposite the sun
Visible because dust, salts, organic aerosols, droplets and molecules scatter light; more particles = stronger rays
practical_applications: Sun ray rules: converge to sun/antisolar point; need haze
limitations: Expert educational site, not peer reviewed; author attribution from site knowledge, not quoted on page

title: Purkinje effect / mesopic vision (Wikipedia; Hanover ISLE simulation) — search summary
key_findings: Photopic peak 555 nm, scotopic peak 507 nm
As light dims reds look darker, blues/greens relatively brighter; mesopic ~0.01-3 cd/m2; colours desaturate
Max scotopic efficacy 1700 lm/W vs 683 lm/W photopic
practical_applications: Night/moonlight colour convention
limitations: Search summary of tertiary sources; underlying CIE standards not read

title: Orders of magnitude (illuminance) and related pages — search summary
key_findings: Full moon ~0.05-0.1 lux typical; table 0.25 lux; up to ~0.32 lux for supermoon in tropics
Moonlight's blue look is perceptual (Purkinje)
practical_applications: Moonlight levels for night scenes
limitations: Values vary by source; direct sunlight lux not confirmed

title: Day for night (Wikipedia; Ira Tiffen DFN filter article in StudentFilmmakers) — search summary
key_findings: Underexpose ~2 stops (ND) and tint blue; warm filters on close shots to keep skin
Avoid showing bright sky
Blue-night convention from stage and silent film; moonlight looks bluish due to Purkinje
practical_applications: Night look in AI/HTML clips
limitations: Search summary; convention not physics

title: Revising the hygroscopicity of inorganic sea salt particles
key_findings: Inorganic sea salt hygroscopic growth 8-15% lower than pure NaCl, likely hydrates
Growth increases for particles <150 nm
Lower hygroscopicity reduced modelled aerosol optical depth by up to 15%
practical_applications: Sea-spray haze physics for Hua Hin beach scenes
limitations: Abstract via search; first author only verified

title: Northern Thailand dry-season PM2.5 / AOD studies (Atmosphere 2023 14(3):538; Int. J. Geoinformatics; Frontiers Env. Sci. 2024) — search summary
key_findings: PM2.5 exceeds Thai standards annually in the dry season (Jan-Apr; other studies Nov-Apr or Feb-May), linked to open burning and satellite AOD
Haze reduces visibility
practical_applications: Dry-season haze look; avoid grading to clear sky in documentary images
limitations: Northern Thailand only, not Hua Hin; abstracts/excerpts only

title: Why Is Water Blue?
authors: Charles L. Braun, Sergei N. Smirnov
key_findings: Water's intrinsic blue from absorption of red by O-H vibrational overtones/combination bands
Visible after several metres; 3 m tube transmits ~44% at 660 nm
Surface appearance also affected by scattering and reflected skylight
practical_applications: Sea colour rules for Hua Hin; shallow vs deep water
limitations: Read as an authorised reprint on webexhibits.org, not the journal page

title: Caustic (optics) (Wikipedia; Atmospheric Optics OPOD) — search summary
key_findings: Caustic = envelope of rays reflected/refracted by a curved surface, or its projection; drinking glass nephroid; pool bottom fold/cusp caustics
Reflective caustics can concentrate sunlight (Vdara hotel)
practical_applications: Lens caustics in sun shadows; caustic projection setup
limitations: Search summary

title: Vision and Rain
key_findings: Photometric model of a rain streak and dynamic model of rain
Rain visibility depends strongly on exposure time and depth of field; camera settings can reduce or enhance it
practical_applications: Rain streak look in clips (shutter -> dots vs streaks)
limitations: Abstract/secondary only

title: Modeling the Interaction of Light Between Diffuse Surfaces
authors: Cindy M. Goral, Kenneth E. Torrance, Donald P. Greenberg, Bennett Battaile
key_findings: Radiosity method from thermal engineering; includes finite-area diffuse sources and colour bleeding from diffuse interreflection; assumes ideal diffuse reflectors (Lambertian in modern terms)
practical_applications: Indirect light and colour bleeding rules
limitations: Abstract only
Spot-check 2026-11-25: original wording checked; finding corrected to match the source.

title: Golden hour (timeanddate.com) and equatorial golden-hour measurements — search summary
key_findings: Golden hour length depends on latitude and season; short near the equator
Measured ~24 min for Singapore at March equinox (0 to +6 degrees)
practical_applications: Cross-check of derived ~25 min golden hour at Hua Hin
limitations: Search summary; definitions vary

title: Raking light (National Gallery glossary; Canadian Conservation Institute; Conservation Wiki) — search summary
authors: National Gallery London; CCI; AIC wiki
key_findings: Single light at a very low angle (~5-10 degrees, CCI) reveals texture/relief by shadows
Use a narrow/point source for crisp shadows; shoot from more than one direction because features parallel to the beam vanish
practical_applications: raking_texture_light setup
limitations: Search summary

title: Book light (StudioBinder; Shane Hurlbut ASC via No Film School; PremiumBeat) — search summary
key_findings: Bounce a hard source into a board, then pass through diffusion: very soft source that keeps shape
Too much gap between bounce and diffusion causes hotspots
practical_applications: book_light_soft_key setup
limitations: Search summary

title: Noon portraits: open shade and scrims (SLR Lounge; Fstoppers; The Phoblographer) — search summary
key_findings: Move subject from overhead noon sun into open shade near its edge
Scrim between sun and subject softens; a scrim can be closer than a reflector so it is softer
Large scrims blow over in wind
practical_applications: tropical_open_shade_sand_bounce and beach_noon_overhead_silk setups
limitations: Search summary; nothing beach-specific

title: Cellulose ester refractive index (patent literature) — search summary
key_findings: Cellulose esters ~1.46-1.50; cellulose acylate 1.48; depends on acetyl substitution; films birefringent
practical_applications: Acetate frame IOR range
limitations: Not eyewear acetate sheet data; search summary

title: Global Solar UV Index: A Practical Guide
key_findings: UVI grouped into low, moderate, high, very high, extreme with colour codes
UV higher closer to the equator; peaks around solar noon
practical_applications: Hua Hin harsh noon context for UV/sun-lens stories
limitations: Numeric category cut-offs not verified (archive PDF failed); equator/noon statements from secondary scans
